strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in diffusion language model reinforcement learning: assigning intermediate credit while keeping probability estimation tractable. Tree rollouts and bottom-up outcome averaging provide a clear, implementable alternative to learned intermediate reward models.

The reported puzzle improvements are substantial even against competing RL methods: at 256 tokens, Sudoku improves from the strongest baseline’s 76.1 to 92.9, and Countdown from 52.4 to 71.1. Comparisons include several recent methods and two evaluation lengths.

Removing self-distillation lowers performance on all four tasks, supporting its practical usefulness. Tree-structure ablations, reverse-schedule experiments, an explicit algorithm, and hardware-specific timing measurements provide useful additional evidence.
weaknesses: The central theoretical interpretation exceeds the bound established in Section 3.3. The confidence gap requires every target token to have high probability both at the parent and across all intermediate orders. Lower average entropy does not establish this condition: confident predictions can disagree across contexts or favor different tokens. Appendix A supports a limiting bound under strong assumptions, not a general monotonic relationship between entropy and actual estimation error. No experiment measures probability-estimation error directly, so the proposed mechanism remains unverified.

The connection between the analyzed probability and the implemented policy update is incomplete. Equation (7) assumes an order distribution Q, but does not derive the marginal transition probability for the actual confidence-dependent token-selection procedure. The analysis also assumes one token per step, whereas experiments decode multiple tokens per step. Moreover, Equations (5) and (16) clip individual token ratios rather than the parent–child transition ratio analyzed in the theory. These choices may define a useful surrogate, but its claimed reliability needs separate justification.

The Math500 data description raises a serious unresolved evaluation concern. Section 4.1 claims official training/test splits, but footnote 3 names ankner/math-500 for training and HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 for testing. MATH-500 is an evaluation subset, and different repository names do not establish disjoint examples. Exact training provenance, sample counts, and an explicit overlap audit are needed before interpreting these results as held-out generalization.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the benefit of intermediate credit assignment from additional sampling and optimization. Changing H or B changes rollout count and compute substantially, yet Figure 3 compares training steps without matched budgets. A flat-rollout baseline with matched completed samples, token budget, and updates is missing. Table 3 also needs clarification: batch time divided by update time implies substantially different update counts across methods despite the stated common gradient-accumulation setting.

Reproducibility is insufficiently specified. Missing details include rollout temperature, training duration and dataset sizes, schedule parameter gamma, clipping and reference-KL coefficients, inner-update counts, parent-group sampling, and reward/prompt implementations. The algorithm does not specify handling empty positive-advantage groups or the zero-temperature endpoint of the distillation schedule. No implementation link is supplied.

Claims of broadly significant gains are stronger than the evidence. GSM8K improvements over the strongest baseline are only 0.1 and 0.2 percentage points, and the method does not lead on 512-token Math500. There are no repeated-run uncertainties or significance analyses. The negative-KL comparator is also not guaranteed to increase entropy, and reverse scheduling alone does not establish superiority over constant-weight distillation. Overall, promising empirical results remain, but the unresolved evaluation, methodological, and reproducibility issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in diffusion language model reinforcement learning: obtaining intermediate credit signals and tractable transition-probability estimates. Tree rollouts with bottom-up outcome averaging provide a concrete, understandable method without requiring a learned process reward model.

The reported puzzle-task improvements are substantial. At 256 tokens, d-TreeRPO achieves 92.9 on Sudoku and 71.1 on Countdown, compared with the strongest reported baselines of 76.1 and 52.4, respectively.

The experiments include six RL baselines, two evaluation lengths, component ablations, tree-parameter sensitivity studies, and training-time measurements. Removing self-distillation lowers reported performance on all four tasks, supporting its practical usefulness within this framework.

The exposition clearly describes the main algorithm and provides pseudocode and an explicit proof. The probability-ratio bound is mathematically reasonable under its stated strong confidence assumptions.
weaknesses: The central theoretical interpretation exceeds what the bound establishes. Section 3.3 requires the same target tokens to have probability near one at the parent state and across every intermediate context and decoding order. Lower average entropy does not establish this condition: different contexts can confidently predict different tokens. Self-distillation at parent states does not guarantee a reduction in the worst-case path uncertainty. The bound tightens as this strong uncertainty measure decreases, but it does not prove that sharpening the policy monotonically reduces actual estimation error. No direct probability-error measurements validate this proposed mechanism.

The connection between the analyzed probability and the implemented optimization needs justification. Equation (7) treats transition probability as an expectation over decoding orders, without deriving the order distribution for the actual confidence-based, multiple-token decoding procedure. That selection mechanism can depend on sampled tokens and the current policy. Furthermore, Equations (5) and (16) clip individual token ratios rather than the joint transition ratio analyzed in Section 3.3. The paper therefore does not establish that its bound controls errors in the optimization actually performed.

The Math500 training protocol raises an important unresolved evaluation concern. Section 4.1 claims official training/test splits, but MATH-500 is an evaluation subset; footnote 3 lists ankner/math-500 for training and HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 for testing. Different dataset repositories do not establish disjoint examples. Exact training provenance, sample counts, and an overlap audit are needed before the mathematical-reasoning results can be trusted. The manuscript alone does not establish whether contamination occurred.

The experiments do not isolate the benefits of intermediate credit assignment from increased sampling and optimization. Changing tree height or branching factor also changes the number of terminal outcomes and computational work, substantially so for the height comparison. A flat-rollout control matched for terminal samples and a comparison matched for compute are missing. Table 3 also needs clarification: batch time divided by update time is approximately 12 for several baselines but 60 for d-TreeRPO, despite the stated common gradient-accumulation setting. Consequently, both the causal explanation and efficiency comparison remain uncertain.

Reproducibility is insufficiently specified. Missing details include rollout sampling temperature, total training steps, scheduling parameter gamma, PPO clipping and reference-KL coefficients, inner-update count, parent-group sampling, and baseline training budgets. The self-distillation equations also require handling empty positive-advantage groups and the zero-temperature schedule endpoint. Dataset sizes, reward-verifier details, and code availability are not supplied sufficiently to resolve these implementation choices.

Evidence for broad reasoning improvements and the scheduling mechanism is limited. Gains over the strongest GSM8K baseline are only 0.1 and 0.2 points, and the method does not lead on 512-token Math500. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. The negative-KL 'diversity' objective does not inherently promote entropy, so its poorer performance is not a clean test of the confidence hypothesis. Constant-weight distillation and direct entropy controls would be more informative. Overall, the promising empirical method merits revision, but unresolved evaluation, reproducibility, and central-claim issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation in its present form.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: reinforcement learning for diffusion language models with tractable probability estimates and finer credit assignment. Tree rollouts and bottom-up outcome averaging provide a clear, implementable approach without requiring a learned process-reward model.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements on puzzle tasks over strong included baselines. At 256 tokens, Sudoku improves from the best baseline’s 76.1 to 92.9, and Countdown from 52.4 to 71.1. These results warrant further investigation.
The self-distillation ablation is useful: removing it reduces performance on all four tasks, supporting its practical contribution within the proposed framework.

The paper includes pseudocode, a detailed conditional probability-bound proof, several architectural ablations, and wall-clock measurements. It also acknowledges the exponential cost of increasing tree depth.
weaknesses: The central theoretical interpretation is stronger than the result supports. Equations (9)–(11) assume that the particular target tokens receive high probability at the parent and along every considered decoding path. Lower entropy does not establish this cross-context agreement: distributions can become confidently inconsistent. The proof establishes a shrinking worst-case bound under that assumption, not monotonically decreasing actual error as entropy falls. No direct probability-error measurements demonstrate that self-distillation produces the claimed mechanism.

The connection between the transition-probability analysis and the optimization objective is incomplete. Equation (4) approximates a joint transition probability with a product, but Equations (5) and (16) clip individual token ratios instead of the corresponding product ratio. This may be a useful surrogate, but the transition-level bound does not establish its policy-gradient accuracy. Moreover, Equation (7)’s distribution over decoding orders needs justification for the actual adaptive, confidence-based sampler.

The Math500 data split raises a material evaluation concern. Section 4.1 claims official training/test splits, but MATH-500 is an evaluation subset, and footnote 3 identifies ankner/math-500 as training data and HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 as test data. The manuscript does not establish that these contain disjoint problems. Exact training provenance and a problem-level overlap audit are necessary; the current description cannot establish uncontaminated mathematical evaluation.

Important reproduction details are missing, including rollout sampling temperature, the scheduling parameter gamma, clipping and reference-KL coefficients, total training budgets, inner-update counts, and reward-verifier specifications. The self-distillation target is also undefined when no child has positive advantage, and its temperature reaches zero at the schedule endpoint without a stated implementation convention.

The experiments do not isolate tree credit assignment from increased sampling and computation. Changing H or B changes the number of leaves exponentially or polynomially, yet Figure 3 compares training steps rather than matched rollout or compute budgets. A matched-budget flat-rollout baseline would make the attribution substantially stronger. The scheduling study also lacks a constant-weight, constant-temperature distillation control.

Statistical support is insufficient for the smaller mathematical gains. At 256 tokens, GSM8K exceeds the best baseline by only 0.1 percentage point; at 512 tokens, Math500 is below the best baseline. Seeds, uncertainty estimates, and result-aggregation procedures are unspecified. The headline gains are against the base model and should not be read as gains over competing RL methods.

Overall, the promising empirical results do not yet overcome the unresolved evaluation-provenance, reproducibility, and central-mechanism concerns. These require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation; the recommendation is not limited merely by subjective novelty or interest.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in diffusion language model training: obtaining useful intermediate credit assignments while keeping likelihood estimation affordable. The tree rollout, bottom-up value estimates, and branch-relative objective form a concrete, understandable approach.

The reported puzzle improvements are substantial across two backbones. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct with 256-token outputs, Sudoku improves from 25.7 for the strongest listed baseline to 92.9, and Countdown from 64.1 to 71.1.

Table 2 provides a valuable control using equal numbers of leaf completions and both tree and independent rollout variants. Table 3 further supports an incremental benefit from self-distillation across all four tasks.

The manuscript includes explicit objectives, prompts, reward definitions, several hyperparameter analyses, and hardware-specific timing measurements. These provide useful foundations for replication and acknowledge the computational cost of branching.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 does not establish the central claim that increasing prediction confidence reduces the relevant estimation error. Its valid inequality assumes that both the single-pass probability and a high-probability lower bound on path-conditioned probabilities are already near one for the same realized token. Lower entropy alone does not ensure this agreement: different contexts can confidently prefer different tokens. The self-distillation objective is not shown to improve the required path quantile. Moreover, the theorem bounds typical path-wise deviations, rather than directly establishing the claimed error bound for the expectation; the exceptional probability mass must also be accounted for.

The probability target underlying the reliability argument needs justification. Equation (3) averages conditionals along permutations of a fixed completion, without establishing that this quantity is the actual marginal token probability or the probability needed for the parent-to-child policy ratio. Confidence-based decoding makes the distribution over orders policy- and state-dependent, while parallel unmasking introduces further distinctions from sequential permutations. Conversely, policy gradients can operate on sampled trajectories using conditional transition probabilities without marginalizing all trajectories. The criticism of trajectory-based methods in Appendix B therefore does not establish that their updates suffer the asserted marginalization defect.

The empirical error analysis does not resolve these theoretical concerns. Table 4 averages the signed quantity log(ptrue/p̂), which can conceal errors through cancellation, rather than reporting absolute or squared error. Its 32 random orders are not shown to follow the rollout distribution Q, and Monte Carlo uncertainty is not assessed. Comparing different converged policies also does not isolate whether improved performance comes from more accurate probability estimates or simply from reinforcing successful outputs.

Dataset and evaluation details leave important reproducibility questions unresolved. Appendix C claims official training/test splits for Math500, but links ankner/math-500 for training and HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 for testing without documenting their relationship or checking overlap. This requires an explicit provenance and disjointness audit; it is not evidence by itself that leakage occurred. Sudoku uses a partial-cell training reward, while evaluation is described as pass@1 without specifying whether the reported score measures complete valid solutions or partial correctness. Dataset sizes, exact training durations, optimizer/update settings, and handling of empty positive-advantage groups are also insufficiently specified.

The controlled experiments remain incomplete for attributing gains. Equal leaf counts in Table 2 do not establish equal optimization or compute budgets, and the treatment of self-distillation in the sparse variants is unclear. Increasing tree height at fixed branching also increases the number of completions exponentially, confounding the granularity interpretation of Figure 4. A constant-weight distillation baseline would help establish the benefit of scheduling; the negative-KL comparator is not inherently an entropy-increasing objective.

There are no reported repeated-run uncertainties for the principal performance comparisons, and plotted training steps lack numerical ticks. This particularly limits interpretation of small mathematical-reasoning gains, such as 81.2 versus 81.1 on GSM8K; the method also does not win every setting. The substantial puzzle results are promising, but the unresolved likelihood justification, evaluation protocol, and reproducibility issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present. These warrant substantive revisions rather than merely a narrower novelty claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: improving reinforcement learning for diffusion language models through intermediate credit assignment and efficient probability estimation. The tree rollout and bottom-up value computation are clearly described and practically motivated.

The reported puzzle-task improvements are substantial across two backbones. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct with 256-token outputs, Sudoku improves from 25.7 for the strongest listed baseline to 92.9, and Countdown from 64.1 to 71.1. These results warrant further investigation.

The experiments include useful controls: equal-leaf-budget sparse-reward variants, removal of self-distillation, decoding-block variations, and training-cost measurements. Table 2 provides meaningful evidence that the gains are not explained solely by generating more completions.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 does not establish the central claim that increasing prediction confidence makes probability estimation more accurate. Its inequality follows from assuming that both the single-pass estimate and the probabilities of the same realized token across most decoding orders are already near one. Lower entropy alone does not ensure this agreement: different contexts can confidently predict different tokens. The self-distillation objective is not shown to reduce the cross-order confidence gap in Eq. (12). Furthermore, the theorem bounds path-wise error on a high-probability event, rather than directly establishing the claimed error bound for the expected probability; the exceptional probability mass must also be accounted for.

The probabilistic target underlying the reliability argument is insufficiently justified. Equations (3) and (23) average token probabilities over orders while inserting a fixed completion's tokens into intermediate states. The paper does not establish that this quantity is the actual marginal token or transition probability under its confidence-based, partially parallel sampler, or that ratios of these quantities yield appropriate importance weights in Eq. (19). The criticism of trajectory-conditioned methods also overlooks that policy gradients can legitimately operate on sampled trajectories without marginalizing over every trajectory producing the same completion.

Table 4 does not adequately validate improved estimation accuracy. It reports the signed quantity log(p_true/p_hat), whose mean can decrease through cancellation rather than smaller absolute error. The reference uses only 32 random orders, without establishing their correspondence to the rollout distribution or reporting Monte Carlo convergence. Comparing different converged policies also leaves unclear whether the same states and tokens are evaluated. Absolute or squared errors on a controlled evaluation set, with uncertainty estimates, would provide stronger evidence.

The Math500 data protocol raises an unresolved evaluation-integrity concern. Appendix C.3 cites ankner/math-500 for training and HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 for testing while claiming official training-test splits. Distinct repository names do not establish disjoint examples, and MATH-500 is an evaluation subset. The paper needs exact split sizes, dataset versions, and a question-level overlap audit. The manuscript alone does not establish leakage, but it also does not establish a valid held-out evaluation.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain incomplete. Important settings such as total training steps, optimizer configuration, PPO clipping and reference-KL coefficients, update reuse, and baseline rollout budgets are not adequately specified. The treatment of nodes with no positive-advantage children is also missing. Equal leaf counts in Table 2 are useful but do not establish equal optimization or computational budgets across the main comparison. Multiple training seeds and uncertainty estimates are absent; several mathematical-reasoning improvements are small, and the method does not outperform every baseline in Table 1.

The ablations support the practical usefulness of the combined method more strongly than its proposed mechanism. Reward-weighted self-training could improve performance without correcting likelihood estimates. A constant-schedule control and a conventional entropy-control baseline would help separate these explanations; the negative-KL diversity objective is not a clean entropy-maximization control. Overall, the promising empirical contribution merits revision, but the unresolved probability formulation, theoretical overclaim, and evaluation/reproducibility gaps prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in diffusion-language-model optimization. Tree-structured rollouts provide an intuitive way to estimate intermediate advantages from verifiable terminal rewards without training an additional critic.

The reported puzzle-task improvements are substantial across both backbones. On LLaDA-8B with 256-token outputs, Sudoku improves from 25.7% for the strongest listed baseline to 92.9%, and Countdown improves from 64.1% to 71.1%.

Table 2 provides useful controls with equal numbers of completed rollouts, including tree sampling without intermediate credit assignment. These results support the practical value of the proposed advantage construction beyond simply generating more completions.

The experimental investigation includes self-distillation ablations, decoding-block variations, scheduling comparisons, hyperparameter sensitivity, and computational costs. Prompts, reward definitions, and several important training settings are supplied.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 does not establish the central claim that increasing model confidence generally improves probability estimation. Its bound assumes that both the single-pass probability and most path-conditioned probabilities are already close to one for the same realized token. Lower entropy or greater confidence alone does not ensure this agreement: different contexts can confidently predict different tokens. The proof is valid under its assumptions, but the paper does not show that self-distillation reduces the required confidence-gap quantity or derive the claimed expectation-error guarantee with its dependence on the exceptional probability δ.

The probability target itself needs justification. Equation (3) averages token conditionals over orders while holding the realized completion fixed; this is not automatically the marginal token probability or transition likelihood of the actual decoder. The relationship to confidence-based, parallel unmasking and the importance ratios in Equation (19) is not established. Likewise, Appendix B treats trajectory-conditioned likelihoods as inherently deficient, although policy-gradient optimization can legitimately operate on sampled trajectories without marginalizing final-output likelihoods.

Table 4 offers suggestive rather than decisive evidence for the proposed mechanism. It reports signed log-ratio means, which can conceal cancellation, rather than absolute or squared estimation errors. The relationship between its 32 random orders and the decoder-induced distribution Q is unclear. Comparing different converged policies also does not isolate whether improved estimation causes the performance gains. A shared evaluation set of states and tokens, appropriate order sampling, and Monte Carlo uncertainty would strengthen this analysis.

The data protocol requires clarification before the mathematical-reasoning results can be trusted fully. Appendix C claims official train/test splits for Math500 but names ankner/math-500 as training data and HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500 as test data. MATH-500 is an evaluation subset; the manuscript needs to identify the actual training examples, their provenance, and an explicit overlap check. This ambiguity is not evidence that leakage occurred, but it is consequential.

Reproduction remains difficult despite the supplied settings. The paper omits clear task-specific training durations, optimizer and update schedules, clipping and reference-KL coefficients, random seeds, and checkpoint-selection procedures. Handling empty positive-advantage sets in self-distillation is unspecified. The training plots lack numerical horizontal-axis ticks, and baseline training budgets and implementations are insufficiently documented.

The broader performance claims exceed the evidence. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, while several mathematical-reasoning improvements over the strongest baselines are only fractions of a percentage point, and d-TreeRPO is not best in every setting. Table 2 controls completed-rollout count but does not establish compute-matched superiority for the main comparisons. Overall, the strong puzzle results justify further consideration, but the central theoretical interpretation and unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues require revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
